passage:
'I deleted the whole club website, sir. The backup too. Three years of stuff.' Akash stared at the floor of the computer lab.
Nilesh sir leaned back in his chair. 'Want to hear something?'
'Not really.'
'When I was sixteen, I wiped my father's shop accounts. Two years of them. I thought I was cleaning up his computer.'
Akash looked up. 'Seriously?'
'He didn't speak to me for a week. We rebuilt it from paper receipts over the whole summer.'
'And you still became a programmer?'
'I became a programmer who makes backups of backups. That mistake taught me more than any class.' He smiled. 'Yours is smaller, by the way. The hosting company keeps copies for thirty days.'
Akash let out a breath he'd been holding since lunch. 'So there's hope.'
'There's always hope. Now pull up a chair. And next time you mess up, find someone who'll tell you theirs.'

qa.q: What did Nilesh sir wipe when he was sixteen?
qa.a: His father's shop accounts, two years of them.

qa.q: What was Akash feeling when Nilesh sir told his story?
qa.a: He felt surprised and then hopeful, letting out a breath he'd held since lunch 🙂

qa.q: What could Akash take from this conversation for the future?
qa.a: Make backups of backups, and look for people who will share their own honest mistakes.

qa.q: Why might Nilesh sir have chosen to share his own story?
qa.a: He likely saw Akash's shame and knew that hearing a worse mistake from a mentor could bring hope.

grounding: Shows a teen ashamed of a big mistake whose mentor shares a worse one from his own youth, bringing hope.

passage: Last March I got caught copying in the half-yearly chemistry exam and was suspended for three days. I'm Jatin, and at the time I honestly thought my life was over. I stayed in my room calling myself a cheat and a loser. On the second evening Irfan bhai, who coaches our colony cricket team, knocked on the door with two cutting chais. He didn't lecture me. He told me that at my age he'd been thrown out of his hostel for starting a fight, and his father had to come and plead with the warden. 'I thought I was finished too,' he said. 'Now I teach twenty kids not to do what I did.' I remember staring at him. Irfan bhai, the calmest person I knew. Something in my chest loosened. It wasn't that my mistake was fine. It was that people come back from worse. Since then I look for grown-ups who tell the truth about themselves. They're rarer than you'd think.

qa.q: Why was Irfan bhai thrown out of his hostel?
qa.a: For starting a fight.

qa.q: What did Jatin feel when Irfan bhai shared his story?
qa.a: Jatin felt surprised and a loosening in the chest, a first hope that people come back from worse.

qa.q: What lesson does Jatin take for the future?
qa.a: To look for grown-ups who tell the truth about their own mistakes.

qa.q: How does Irfan bhai seem to see his old mistake now?
qa.a: As something that shaped him into someone who teaches kids not to repeat it.

grounding: A first-person memory of a teen ashamed after being suspended, given hope by a mentor who shares a worse mistake of his own.

passage: Elizabeth smiled at Tushar across the college library on Monday, and by Tuesday he had planned their whole future: a flat in Pune, a dog, her parents adoring him. The trouble was, he knew almost nothing about her except that she studied economics and liked the window seat. And she was leaving for a three-month internship in Bengaluru on Friday. Every text she sent, 'thanks for the notes!', he read ten times, asking his roommate what the exclamation mark meant. On Wednesday night, heart hammering, he caught himself drafting a long message about 'feelings'. He deleted it. This was a feeling, not a fact. He didn't really know her. On Thursday he walked up to her in the library and asked, simply, 'Want to get chai before you leave? I'd like to actually get to know you.' She laughed. 'Sure. Also, you realise I'm terrible at replying to texts?' He had not realised. That was the first real thing he learned about her.

qa.q: When was Elizabeth leaving for her internship?
qa.a: On Friday, for three months in Bengaluru.

qa.q: What was Tushar feeling as he read her texts ten times?
qa.a: He felt giddy and anxious, his heart racing, building meaning out of tiny signs.

qa.q: What did Tushar do instead of sending the long message?
qa.a: He asked Elizabeth directly for chai to get to know the real person, rather than decoding texts.

qa.q: How might Elizabeth see Tushar's simple invitation?
qa.a: As friendly and easy to accept, which is why she laughs and says sure.

grounding: Shows a young man idealising a crush from small signs, then choosing to get to know her and ask directly instead of decoding texts.

passage: Every time Vinita replied to one of Gurpreet's stories with a laughing face, he spent the metro ride from Rajiv Chowk to Dwarka building a whole life: introducing her to his Biji, a Punjabi-Maharashtrian wedding, two kids. They had spoken maybe five times, all about the civil services coaching notes. On Saturday she replied 'haha same' to his post about burnt rotis, and he sent a screenshot to his friend Manpreet with the caption: 'what does this MEAN.' Manpreet wrote back: 'It means she also burns rotis, bro.' Gurpreet laughed, then sat with it. His heart raced, sure. But he was falling for a highlight reel he had written himself. After Monday's class he caught up with Vinita on the stairs. 'Hey, do you actually burn rotis, or were you being nice?' 'Every single time,' she grinned. They talked all the way to the metro. It was ordinary and awkward and much better than the fantasy.

qa.q: What did Vinita reply to Gurpreet's post about burnt rotis?
qa.a: 'haha same'.

qa.q: What was Gurpreet feeling as he built a future on the metro rides?
qa.a: He felt excited and infatuated, his heart racing over small signs from someone he barely knew.

qa.q: Which choice worked for Gurpreet, and why?
qa.a: Talking to Vinita directly about something real, which replaced his fantasy with an actual conversation 🙂

qa.q: How does Manpreet see the 'haha same' reply?
qa.a: As a simple reply about burnt rotis, not a hidden message, which helps Gurpreet laugh at his decoding.

grounding: Shows a young man idealising a crush from small online signs, then choosing to get to know her directly instead of decoding.

passage: In the chemistry lab at her college in Nagpur, Rajni found the third anonymous chocolate in her drawer that week, this one with a note: 'You have the best laugh in B-batch. - M.' It didn't take long to work out: Manoj, the quiet boy from the next bench, went red every time she looked his way. She felt flattered and awkward at once. Her roommate said, 'Keep him guessing, it's fun,' and another friend wanted to post the note in the batch group. Rajni didn't want either. She didn't feel the same, and she didn't want him hoping for weeks. After practicals she waited until the lab emptied. 'Manoj, thank you for the notes. That was really sweet. But I don't feel that way, and I didn't want to leave you guessing.' He nodded, ears burning. 'Okay. Thanks for saying it straight.' She put the notes away somewhere private and never showed them to anyone.

qa.q: What did the third note say?
qa.a: 'You have the best laugh in B-batch. - M.'

qa.q: How did Rajni feel on finding the chocolates and notes?
qa.a: She felt flattered and awkward at once.

qa.q: What did Rajni do that was kind and clear?
qa.a: She told Manoj privately, thanked him, said she didn't feel the same, and kept his notes private instead of mocking him.

qa.q: How does Manoj take Rajni's answer?
qa.a: He's embarrassed, ears burning, but grateful she said it straight instead of leaving him guessing.

grounding: Shows a young woman liked by someone she barely knows, feeling flattered and awkward, and giving a kind, clear, private no early.

passage:
Hi Karthik,
Thank you for your message on Sunday. I've read it a few times, and I want to answer properly rather than leave it hanging.
It honestly made my day to know someone noticed the little things, like how I always bring extra pens to the design studio. That was kind of you to say, and brave.
But I need to be clear: I don't have those feelings for you. We've only talked a handful of times, and I don't want to say 'maybe later' when I know that isn't true. That wouldn't be fair to you.
I haven't shown your message to anyone, and I won't. I'd be glad to keep saying hi in studio and sharing pens, if that feels comfortable for you. If you need some space, I understand that too.
Take care,
Sabina

qa.q: What little thing did Karthik notice?
qa.a: That Sabina always brings extra pens to the design studio.

qa.q: How did Karthik's message make Sabina feel?
qa.a: Sabina felt flattered and touched, even as saying no felt awkward.

qa.q: What makes Sabina's reply kind and clear?
qa.a: It thanks Karthik, gives a direct no without false hope, and promises privacy and space.

qa.q: How might Karthik feel reading the email?
qa.a: Disappointed but respected, since Sabina answered honestly and kept the message private.

grounding: An email from a young person liked by someone they barely know, answering kindly and clearly without leaving false hope or mocking.

passage: Tanvir, you're sending your friend to ask her if she likes you? Let your Sachin Mama tell you something. At twenty, in engineering college in Surat, I liked a girl called Leela from the library for a whole year. A whole year! Every time I got close, I pictured her laughing, the whole hostel finding out, and my legs turned to stone. So I hinted. I left song lyrics in her books. I sent my roommate to 'find out'. She thought he liked her, which was a disaster. Finally, in the last month of college, my friend Mehul said, 'She might say no. That will hurt. It will not kill you.' So I walked up and said, 'Leela, would you like to get tea with me?' Just that. She said, 'Sorry, Sachin, I'm seeing someone.' It stung for a week. Then it was done, and I could breathe again. Ask her yourself, once, simply. That's all.

qa.q: Who did Sachin send to 'find out' about Leela?
qa.a: His roommate.

qa.q: What was Sachin feeling every time he got close to Leela?
qa.a: He felt frozen with fear, picturing her laughing and the whole hostel finding out.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Sachin's story?
qa.a: Mehul's words that a no would hurt but not kill him, which led Sachin to ask Leela simply, once.

qa.q: How did Leela seem to read the song lyrics and the roommate?
qa.a: She misread them, thinking the roommate liked her, which shows how hinting confused things.

grounding: An elder's story of freezing out of fear of rejection, hinting and using a messenger, then asking simply once and surviving the no.

passage: It was the last evening of the college fest, and Aparna was leaving for her hometown in Kolkata the next morning for two months. Tarun had rehearsed the question all day. Every time he walked towards her stall, he imagined her polite smile, her friends giggling, the story spreading through the hostel, and he veered off to buy another cold coffee. By nine the stalls were packing up and the loudspeakers were blaring. His friend Nikhil offered, 'Should I just ask her for you?' Tarun almost said yes. Then he shook his head. If she said no, it would hurt, but it wouldn't be the end of him. He walked over and said, above the noise, 'Aparna, I like you. Would you want to go for coffee when you're back?' She blinked, then smiled. 'I'd like that. Save my number properly this time.' He walked back with shaking hands and three cold coffees too many.

qa.q: Where was Aparna going the next morning?
qa.a: To her hometown in Kolkata, for two months.

qa.q: Why did Tarun keep veering off to buy cold coffee?
qa.a: He was afraid of rejection, imagining her polite smile and the story spreading through the hostel.

qa.q: What did Tarun do instead of letting Nikhil ask for him?
qa.a: He asked Aparna himself, simply and once, accepting that a no would hurt but not define him.

qa.q: How does Aparna respond to Tarun's direct question?
qa.a: She seems pleasantly surprised and says yes, asking him to save her number properly 😊

grounding: Shows a young man frozen by fear of rejection who refuses to use a friend as messenger and asks his crush simply, once.

passage:
'Uma, can I say something weird?' Seema asked, stopping on the hostel stairs.
'Weird is my favourite.'
'I think I like you. As more than a friend. For a while now.'
Uma's stomach flipped. She had half guessed. She sat down on the step. 'Thank you for telling me. That took guts.'
'But?'
'But I don't feel the same way. I've thought about it, because I love being your friend and I didn't want to answer carelessly. It's not a maybe.'
Seema looked away. 'Okay. That stings.'
'I know. I'm sorry it stings. I'm not going to pretend it's about exams or timing. It's just not how I feel.'
'Thanks for not making up a reason.'
'Do you want some space? I'll understand. I'll still be here after.'
Seema gave a wobbly laugh. 'Maybe a week. Then we go back to arguing about films.'
'Deal.'

qa.q: Where did Seema tell Uma about her feelings?
qa.a: On the hostel stairs.

qa.q: What was Uma feeling when Seema said she liked her?
qa.a: Her stomach flipped; she felt nervous and caring, not wanting to hurt her friend.

qa.q: What made Uma's no gracious?
qa.a: She thanked Seema, gave a clear no without fake reasons like exams or timing, and offered space without false hope.

qa.q: How does Seema take Uma's answer?
qa.a: It stings, but she's grateful Uma didn't make up a reason, and asks for a week before going back to normal.

grounding: Shows a young woman giving a friend a gracious, honest no to romantic feelings, without fake reasons or false hope.

passage: In my second year of college, a boy from my statistics class, Nitin, told me he liked me. I'm Elizabeth, and I'm not proud of the next month. I didn't feel the same, but I liked being liked. So I replied to his late-night texts with hearts, let him buy me coffee, and said 'let's see' when he asked. My friend Sangeeta watched this and finally said, 'You know he's planning your birthday, right? Is that fair?' It hit hard. I'd been keeping him around because it felt nice to be wanted. The next day I asked Nitin to sit with me on the library steps. I said, 'I'm sorry. I should have said this at the start. I don't feel that way about you, and I let you think maybe. That wasn't fair.' He was quiet, then said, 'I kind of knew.' It stung both of us. But it was the first honest thing I'd given him.

qa.q: What did Elizabeth say when Nitin first asked?
qa.a: 'Let's see'.

qa.q: What was Elizabeth feeling when Sangeeta spoke up?
qa.a: Elizabeth felt a hard jolt of guilt, seeing that the attention had been kept going just because it felt nice.

qa.q: What should Elizabeth have done at the start?
qa.a: Given a clear, kind no right away instead of hearts and 'let's see'.

qa.q: How did Nitin seem to feel when Elizabeth finally spoke honestly?
qa.a: Hurt but not surprised, saying he 'kind of knew', which shows the vagueness had been confusing him.

grounding: A first-person account of leading someone on for the attention, then giving an honest, gracious no without false hope.

passage: Karthik had said no kindly, on Friday, outside the college canteen: he liked Pooja as a friend, nothing more. By Saturday she had typed and deleted six messages. 'Are you sure?' 'Was it something I did?' 'You were so nice to me, what was that then?' The problem: they were in the same four-person project group, and the final presentation was on Wednesday. She couldn't disappear. She felt small, and stupid, and angry, and underneath it all just sad. On Sunday she called her cousin Sneha and cried for an hour. Sneha didn't tell her to get over it. She said, 'Grieve it. Just don't chase it.' So Pooja deleted the drafts and muted Karthik's stories for a while. At Monday's group meeting she kept to slides and deadlines, polite, a little quiet. When a friend whispered, 'Didn't he lead you on?' Pooja shook her head. 'No. He was just kind. I misread it.'

qa.q: When was the project's final presentation?
qa.a: On Wednesday.

qa.q: What was Pooja feeling after Karthik's no?
qa.a: She felt small, stupid and angry, and underneath it all, sad 😔

qa.q: What helped Pooja avoid chasing Karthik?
qa.a: Crying it out with Sneha, deleting the drafts, muting his stories and keeping group work polite.

qa.q: How might Karthik feel at Monday's meeting?
qa.a: Probably relieved that Pooja stayed polite and professional, without blame or pressure.

grounding: Shows a young woman turned down by a crush who grieves, stops chasing, takes distance and refuses to blame him, despite sharing a project.

passage: Nirmala had told Yogesh, gently, at the Andheri bus stop, that she didn't feel the same. For three days he sulked. He left her messages on 'seen', skipped the study group, and when his roommate asked, he muttered, 'She kept talking to me, what was I supposed to think?' On the fourth night, scrolling through her profile for the twentieth time, he caught himself. What was he doing? She had never promised him anything. She had just been friendly. It hurt; that part was real. But the sulking and blaming were making him feel worse, not better. He put the phone in a drawer and went for a run along Juhu road until his chest ached for a different reason. The next day he rejoined the study group, said a normal 'hi' to Nirmala and sat at the other end of the table. He'd need time. He would give himself that, without making her pay for it.

qa.q: Where did Nirmala tell Yogesh she didn't feel the same?
qa.a: At the Andheri bus stop.

qa.q: What was Yogesh feeling during the three days of sulking?
qa.a: He felt hurt and rejected, which came out as sulking and blaming Nirmala.

qa.q: What changed in how Yogesh handled the rejection?
qa.a: He stopped scrolling and blaming, went for a run, and returned to the study group while keeping some distance.

qa.q: How might Nirmala have felt when Yogesh left her messages on 'seen'?
qa.a: Probably uneasy and a little guilty, even though she had only been friendly and honest.

grounding: Shows a young man turned down who first sulks and blames, then grieves, stops chasing and takes distance without blame.

passage: In the university library, Lavanya had opened the same economics chapter four times without reading a line. Her phone lay beside the book, Imran's profile open. Online 3 minutes ago. New story: a cricket match. Who was he with? Why hadn't he replied to her meme? She had read his mood into his emojis at least twenty times that day. At seven she found herself packing her bag to walk past the boys' hostel gate, 'just in case' he was there. She stopped on the library steps. This wasn't about Imran; they'd had three conversations. It was about the not-knowing, and the story she kept writing in her head. Turning up at his hostel uninvited would be crossing a line. She sat on a bench and called her friend Ruchi. 'I think I'm a bit obsessed, and I hate it.' Ruchi said, 'Come to badminton with me tonight. And tomorrow. Let's make your life bigger than one profile.'

qa.q: What did Imran's profile show when Lavanya checked it?
qa.a: Online 3 minutes ago, and a new story of a cricket match.

qa.q: What was Lavanya feeling as she packed her bag to walk past his hostel?
qa.a: She felt restless and anxious, caught in a loop of wondering, driven by the not-knowing.

qa.q: What did Lavanya do instead of going to the hostel gate?
qa.a: She stopped, recognised the fantasy, called Ruchi, and agreed to fill her evenings with badminton.

qa.q: How might Imran feel if Lavanya had turned up uninvited?
qa.a: Probably uncomfortable or uneasy, since they had only had three conversations.

grounding: Shows a young woman whose crush has become an obsessive loop, noticing the fantasy, stopping before turning up uninvited and widening her life.

passage:
Dear Apa,
I need to tell someone, and you're the one person who won't laugh.
You know Pankaj from my internship? We've had lunch twice. That's it. But for a month I've been checking his profile every hour, reading his old posts from years ago, noticing which colour hearts he uses. Last week I caught myself taking a longer route to work because I'd worked out from his check-ins that he buys coffee at that corner. When I realised I was timing it, I felt sick.
I don't even know him. I know a version I made up at 2 a.m.
So I've done a few things. I've muted him. I've joined the Saturday pottery class you kept suggesting. I'm back on my usual route.
It's hard. The loop still starts. But it gets shorter when I do other things.
Can we talk on Sunday? I think saying it out loud would help.
Love,
Nazia

qa.q: What did Nazia work out from Pankaj's check-ins?
qa.a: That he buys coffee at a particular corner.

qa.q: What did Nazia feel on realising the route was being timed?
qa.a: Nazia felt sick and alarmed at the obsessive pattern.

qa.q: What steps did Nazia take to widen life beyond the crush?
qa.a: Muted Pankaj, joined the Saturday pottery class, went back to the usual route, and asked Apa to talk.

qa.q: How might Pankaj feel if he noticed Nazia timing the route to his coffee stop?
qa.a: He would likely feel uneasy and watched, since they had only had lunch twice.

grounding: A letter from a young person caught in an obsessive loop over a crush, noticing the fantasy, stopping the tracking and widening their life.

passage:
Dear Mrs Kulkarni,
Thank you for telling me on the phone this morning that you've already alerted the gate guard and will call the proctor's office today. As you asked, here are the details in writing.
Since September, a student from the engineering block, Deepak, has been messaging me many times a day. On 3 October I told him clearly, once, in writing: 'I'm not interested. Please stop contacting me.' I haven't replied since.
He hasn't stopped. He's sent over forty messages from new numbers, and twice this week he waited outside our hostel gate at night. Yesterday he left a note on my cycle.
I've kept screenshots of every message with dates, and the note; copies are attached. My roommate has seen him at the gate too.
I feel uneasy walking alone now. I know this isn't my fault, but I wanted it on record.
Thank you,
Hansa, Room 214

qa.q: What did Hansa write to Deepak on 3 October?
qa.a: 'I'm not interested. Please stop contacting me.'

qa.q: How does Hansa feel now about walking alone?
qa.a: Hansa feels uneasy and anxious walking alone after Deepak waited at the gate.

qa.q: What steps did Hansa take that fit the situation?
qa.a: Said no clearly once, stopped replying, kept dated screenshots and the note, and reported to the warden.

qa.q: How does Mrs Kulkarni respond to the report?
qa.a: She takes it seriously, alerting the gate guard and calling the proctor's office the same day.

grounding: A letter reporting unwanted, intense attention after one clear no, with records kept and the warden involved; it is not the writer's fault.

passage: Imran, you asked why I switched cafés. Okay, here's the whole thing. I'm Aditi, and for a month a guy from my photography club kept messaging me. At first it was just 'nice shot!' Then twenty messages a day, voice notes at 2 a.m., and then he started turning up at the café where I study and sitting at the next table. I felt watched all the time. I kept thinking, did I encourage this? I'd liked his photos once. My cousin said, 'That's not on you. Say no once, clearly, then stop.' So I messaged him: 'I'm not interested in anything more. Please stop messaging and don't come to my café.' I took screenshots of everything first, dates and all, then blocked him. When he appeared at the club meeting and tried to corner me, I told the club coordinator and the student welfare office that same day. They've spoken to him. It wasn't my fault. That's the part I keep reminding myself.

qa.q: Where did the club member start turning up?
qa.a: At the café where Aditi studies, at the next table.

qa.q: How did Aditi feel as the attention grew?
qa.a: Aditi felt watched and uneasy, and even wondered guiltily whether it had been encouraged.

qa.q: Which steps did Aditi follow, and why do they help?
qa.a: A clear no once, saving screenshots, blocking, and telling the coordinator and welfare office, so adults could act with evidence.

qa.q: How does Aditi's cousin see the situation?
qa.a: As not Aditi's fault, advising one clear no and then no more contact.

grounding: A spoken account of a young person facing intense, unwanted attention who says no once, stops replying, keeps records and reports it.

passage: In Palampur, Aadhya's phone was her window to Rehan, a boy from a college in Chandigarh she'd met in an online poetry group. His posts were perfect: sunsets, tea, lines of old Urdu poetry, a guitar. In three months of messages he never seemed tired or rude. Aadhya began comparing every boy in town to him and finding them dull. When Rehan came up to Palampur for a family wedding, he suggested meeting. Aadhya panicked. 'What if he isn't him?' Her friend Dolma, weighing tea at her father's shop, laughed. 'He won't be. He'll be a real person. That's the point.' They met at the bus stand dhaba, ordinary as anything. Rehan was shorter than his photos, talked with his mouth full and argued about cricket. For a moment Aadhya felt let down. Then he made her laugh about his aunt's wedding dance, and she realised she liked the real one more. They walked round the tea gardens.

qa.q: Where did Aadhya and Rehan meet in person?
qa.a: At the bus stand dhaba.

qa.q: What was Aadhya feeling when Rehan suggested meeting?
qa.a: She panicked, anxious that the real person wouldn't match the perfect image.

qa.q: What was wise about how Aadhya reacted when Rehan turned out less perfect?
qa.a: She stayed and got to know him instead of dropping him, and found she liked the real person more 😊

qa.q: How does Dolma see Aadhya's online crush?
qa.a: As an image that will naturally differ from the real person, which she thinks is the point of meeting.

grounding: Shows a young woman with an idealised online crush who meets him in an ordinary place, notices the gap and chooses the real person.

passage: For eight months Yuki knew Ivan through a screen: video calls from his neat desk in Prague, photos of snowy bridges, voice notes in careful English that made her smile on the Osaka train. He seemed endlessly patient, always funny. When he finally visited for two weeks in spring, reality arrived with his suitcase. He was grumpy before coffee. He got lost reading train maps and snapped at her once. He left socks on her friend's sofa. On the fourth night Yuki lay awake thinking, this isn't the Ivan I fell for. Part of her wanted to end it right then. Then she remembered: she had only ever seen his best hour of every day. She'd shown him her best hour too. The next morning she said, 'I think we both edited ourselves. Can we just be normal together for a bit?' He laughed, relieved. They spent the day doing laundry and buying groceries. It was the best day of the visit.

qa.q: How long did Ivan visit Osaka?
qa.a: Two weeks, in spring.

qa.q: What was Yuki feeling on the fourth night?
qa.a: She felt disappointed and unsettled, tempted to end it because Ivan wasn't the man she had imagined.

qa.q: What did Yuki suggest instead of ending it?
qa.a: That they stop editing themselves and spend ordinary time together, which they did with laundry and groceries.

qa.q: How does Ivan react to Yuki's suggestion?
qa.a: He laughs, relieved, as if he had also felt the pressure of the perfect image.

grounding: Shows a young woman whose long-distance crush seemed perfect, noticing the gap during a visit and choosing ordinary time with the real person.

passage: College counselling notes, Wednesday. Sabina (second year, design) came in today unsure how to handle feelings for her closest friend, Dhruv. They've been friends since first year: same studio, same late-night chai runs. Over the past months she has realised she's in love with him, and she is terrified of losing the friendship. She admitted she's been snappy with him lately, and felt resentful when he mentioned another girl, then guilty about it. We talked through both paths: staying silent and carrying it, or telling him honestly with no pressure for an answer. She decided the resentment was already harming the friendship. She practised saying, 'I've started feeling more than friendship. You don't owe me anything back. I just didn't want to hide it and get weird with you.' She plans to tell him this weekend and said she will accept either answer. We'll meet again next week.

qa.q: How long have Sabina and Dhruv been friends?
qa.a: Since first year, sharing a studio and late-night chai runs.

qa.q: What has Sabina been feeling lately towards Dhruv?
qa.a: She's been terrified of losing him, and resentful and then guilty when he mentioned another girl.

qa.q: What did Sabina decide, and why is it wise?
qa.a: To tell Dhruv honestly without pressure, because hiding it was already turning into resentment and harming the friendship.

qa.q: How might Dhruv feel hearing Sabina's words?
qa.a: Surprised perhaps, but not pressured, since she makes clear he owes her nothing back.

grounding: A counsellor's note on a young woman who realises she loves her close friend and chooses to tell him without pressure, ready for either answer.

passage: Saturday night. I did it. I told Charu. We were sitting on the ghats in Varanasi after the evening aarti, the same spot we've sat on since Class 11, and I said, 'I think I've fallen for you. You don't have to say anything now. I just didn't want to keep pretending and end up angry at you for not guessing.' He went very quiet. Then he said, 'Bhavna, you're my favourite person. I don't feel it that way. And I'm scared of losing you too.' It hurt. I cried a bit in the rickshaw home. But I also felt lighter, like I'd put down something heavy I'd been carrying since Diwali. I'd been so snappy with him for weeks, and now I know why. Tomorrow we're meeting for kachori as usual. I told him I might need a little distance some days, and he said that's okay. We'll work out the friendship. I'm glad I didn't hide it.
